title: What Does It Really Mean to Be a Good Man?
deck: Character is formed in the choices that rarely make the headlines.

blocks.title: A fictional conversation
blocks.text: This Q&A is an invented editorial example with a fictional father, Daniel. It demonstrates an interview layout; these are not statements from a real interviewee.

We often describe a good man through what he provides. But what happens when provision becomes the only language he knows? In this imagined conversation, Daniel, a father learning to be more present, talks about the work nobody can put on a résumé.
The conversation

blocks.question: When did your idea of being a good man begin to change?
blocks.answer: When I realised I could be reliable at work and unreliable emotionally at home. I remembered every deadline but kept postponing difficult conversations with people I loved. I had to stop treating presence as something I would offer after everything else was finished.

blocks.question: What did taking responsibility look like that week?
blocks.answer: One apology without a defence attached. I told my brother I had dismissed him. Then I listened. Nothing dramatic happened. We made dinner. It felt small, but I had finally stopped trying to win the conversation.

blocks.alt: Open landscape beneath a wide sky
blocks.caption: Illustrative landscape. A pause between questions.

blocks.text: I had finally stopped trying to win the conversation.

blocks.question: Where does faith fit into that?
blocks.answer: It gives me somewhere to bring the gap between the man I announce and the man I actually am. Reflection matters, but so does repairing what I damaged. For me, a prayer has to make room for a phone call afterwards.

blocks.question: What would you tell someone who feels behind?
blocks.answer: Choose one relationship and one promise. Make the promise small enough to keep. You do not need to become an impressive new person by Friday. You need to become a little more trustworthy today.

blocks.text: One question to take away
Who receives the least patient version of you—and what would a more generous response look like this evening?

title: Discipline Is a Spiritual Practice
deck: Make room for what matters through small, repeatable acts of attention.

blocks.text: A useful routine should fit an ordinary Tuesday. Use this seven-day practice to turn an intention into something you can repeat without turning your whole life into a productivity project.
Before you begin
Choose one practice: ten quiet minutes, a short walk, a page of reading or a call you keep delaying. Set a minimum that still feels possible on a difficult day. Completing the minimum counts.

blocks.title: Set up your week
items: Name the practice in one clear sentence.
Choose a cue already in your day, such as finishing breakfast.
Put what you need within reach the night before.
Decide on a two-minute version for a hard day.
Tell one trusted person what you are trying.

blocks.title: Seven small returns
items: Monday: begin, even if it feels awkward.
Tuesday: repeat at the same cue.
Wednesday: notice the obstacle without judging yourself.
Thursday: adjust the environment rather than adding pressure.
Friday: use the small version if you need it.
Sunday: look back and choose what to carry forward.

blocks.text: The practice is returning, not protecting a perfect streak.
Review, then repeat

Ask what made the practice easier, what repeatedly got in the way and whether the minimum was realistic. Keep one useful change. If you missed a day, resume at the next cue rather than doubling the task.

blocks.title: A practice, not a score
blocks.text: These checkboxes are for this reading session. They are not a saved habit tracker, a spiritual ranking or a measure of your worth.

title: The Father You Want to Become
deck: Presence grows through the ordinary moments we choose to share.

blocks.text: In this fictional family vignette, a father has promised his daughter a Saturday without errands. There is no grand destination. There is a walk, a sandwich and the uncomfortable discovery that leaving a phone alone can feel like work.
09:10 / The door

He checks his pocket twice before they leave. Keys, wallet, phone. His daughter is already outside, describing a route that apparently includes every interesting stone on their street. He starts to tell her they are late, then remembers there is nothing to be late for.

blocks.alt: Open landscape beneath a wide sky
blocks.caption: 01 / Leaving the timetable behind. Illustrative stock landscape; not the family in this story.

blocks.text: 11:35 / The long way

She asks why he works so much. He reaches for the polished answer about providing. Instead he says that sometimes he finds work easier to understand than being at home. She considers this, then asks whether he can carry her bag. It is a practical beginning.

blocks.caption: 02 / A little more room. Illustrative stock photograph.

blocks.text: At lunch he lets the silence last. He does not turn the afternoon into a lesson. They watch a dog refuse to return a ball. For once, he has no advice to give anyone.
16:20 / Back home

Nothing has been transformed by the time they reach the door. Monday will still be busy. But when she asks about next Saturday, he opens the calendar with her beside him. They put something small in it and leave the rest blank.

blocks.caption: 03 / Presence is an ordinary promise, kept again. Illustrative stock photograph.

blocks.title: Try a smaller promise
blocks.text: Set aside one unhurried hour with someone you care for. Let them help decide what happens in it. The point is shared attention, not an impressive itinerary.

title: Is Ambition Slowly Destroying Your Peace?
deck: A reflection on achievement, stewardship and knowing when enough is enough.

blocks.text: When every opportunity feels urgent, choosing a direction becomes difficult. This 30-minute review gives you a way to decide what deserves the next season of your attention.

blocks.title: What you need
blocks.text: A sheet of paper, your calendar and 30 minutes. This is a personal planning exercise, not financial advice.

blocks.title: Write the real commitments
blocks.text: Spend five minutes listing what you are already responsible for: work, care, money, health and relationships. Include the invisible jobs. A plan built around an imaginary empty calendar will not survive the week.

blocks.title: Name the price of the next yes
blocks.text: Choose the opportunity occupying your thoughts. Write what it would require in hours and attention, and what would receive less of you. Use actual trade-offs instead of a vague promise to work harder.

blocks.title: Choose a definition of enough
blocks.text: Complete this sentence: for the next three months, progress would mean ____. Choose an outcome you can recognise. Being more successful is too slippery; finishing a proposal or protecting two evenings is easier to assess.

blocks.title: Make one deliberate no
blocks.text: Identify a meeting, project or self-imposed obligation that no longer serves that direction. Decline or renegotiate it clearly. Do not fill the space immediately.

blocks.title: Book the review
blocks.text: Put a 15-minute review in your calendar two weeks from now. Ask whether the plan is making you more dependable and whether the cost still makes sense. Revise the plan when the evidence changes.
A worked example

A fictional designer has three side projects and wants a promotion. His next three months become one portfolio case study, one conversation with his manager and two evenings at home each week. He pauses the other projects. The plan is smaller, but it can now be tested against his actual life.

blocks.title: Before you close the notebook
items: One priority has a clear finish line.
Its cost appears in the calendar.
One competing commitment has been removed.

title: Finding Faith When Life Comes Apart
deck: An editorial reflection on asking for help and beginning again.

blocks.title: Fictional first-person story
blocks.text: This narrative is an original fiction written to demonstrate a longer personal essay with two photographs. It is not a reader testimony.

The first morning after the job ended, I still woke at six. I made coffee, dressed and opened my laptop. There was no meeting to join. The silence felt less like freedom than a question I had spent years avoiding.
The answer I kept giving

For the first week I said I was taking some time out. It was a useful sentence: tidy, voluntary, almost enviable. My friend did not challenge it. He just kept asking whether I wanted to walk on Thursday.

On the third Thursday I told him I was embarrassed. Not simply worried about bills, though I was. Embarrassed that I could no longer introduce myself through a job title. We kept walking. He did not offer a quotation about closed doors.

blocks.caption: An unfamiliar horizon. Illustrative photograph; not a location from a reported account.

blocks.text: Something smaller than certainty

I expected faith to arrive as an explanation. Instead, what helped was a routine: breakfast before emails, a walk before another application, an honest conversation before another polished update. None of these actions solved the uncertainty. They made it possible to live inside it.
I did not need a better announcement. I needed a more honest day.

I began writing down what I could do that afternoon. Some days it was an application. Some days it was asking a former colleague for feedback. On the days when shame made everything heavy, it was answering the friend who had kept checking in.

blocks.caption: The ordinary work of another morning. Illustrative stock photograph.

blocks.text: An unfinished ending

There is no triumphant final paragraph in the notebook from that month. The next job had not appeared. What had changed was the list of people who knew the truth. I had stopped making uncertainty a private performance.

If I could speak to the version of myself at that first empty desk, I would not promise a quick turnaround. I would tell him to eat breakfast, pick up the phone and let someone walk beside him before he knew where the road would lead.

title: Make Room for Rest
deck: An invitation to give recovery a place in your week.

blocks.text: Before turning rest into another assignment, try giving your attention to one quiet thing. This page demonstrates a video-led feature with a playable clip, a description and a short companion practice.

blocks.title: Flower close-up: sample video player
blocks.caption: Player demonstration · MDN flower clip. This media fixture is not a Menclave production.
blocks.description: A short close-up flower clip used by MDN to demonstrate browser video playback. There is no spoken interview or Menclave narration. Use the native playback controls to pause, replay or enter full screen.

blocks.text: A minute without an outcome

Sit somewhere comfortable. Put your phone out of reach if you can. Notice what your attention moves towards when nothing is asking for a response. You do not have to clear your mind or produce an insight.

blocks.title: Let one task wait
blocks.text: Choose something non-urgent and give yourself a definite time to return to it. A boundary is easier to trust when it has a beginning and an end.

blocks.title: Return gently
blocks.text: When the pause ends, notice whether you need water, food, company or a quieter evening. Treat the observation as information rather than another target.

blocks.title: For the finished feature
blocks.text: Replace the demonstration clip with the licensed Menclave film and supply captions and a transcript for any spoken content. The player does not autoplay.

title: The Art of Living with Intention
deck: A thoughtful approach to the spaces and objects of everyday life.

blocks.text: A room does not need to look like a showroom to support the life happening inside it. This visual essay uses four illustrative photographs to explore space, light and the things we choose to keep.
Less to manage, more to notice

Start with the place where your day begins. What do you reach for? What do you move out of the way? A useful space makes ordinary actions easier. The photographs below are visual references, not a documented tour of one home.

images.alt: A shared interior with desks and seating
images.caption: 01 / Space to work. Leave one surface ready for the next task.

images.alt: Clothing arranged as a style reference
images.caption: 02 / Things in use. Choose what serves your actual week.
03 / A wider view. Give the eye somewhere to rest.
04 / A slower start. Notice the light before the notifications.

blocks.text: One useful edit
Choose one corner, drawer or daily routine. Remove what repeatedly gets in the way. Put one useful thing where it belongs. Live with the change for a week before buying a solution.
A well-used life will leave things out of place. Make room for that, too.

title: Learning to Listen Across Differences
deck: Curiosity and conviction can share the same conversation.

blocks.text: Listening gets harder when a disagreement starts to feel like a verdict on who we are. Before planning your response, try finding the experience underneath the other person’s position.
Stay with the actual conversation
Ask what led them to see it that way. You are not promising agreement. You are giving yourself a better chance of understanding what is being said, rather than arguing with the version you expected.

blocks.alt: Open landscape beneath a wide sky
blocks.caption: Room for a different perspective. Illustrative stock photograph.

blocks.title: A sentence to try
blocks.text: I think I understand your conclusion. What happened that made this matter to you?
Take it into the room

The linked conversation is a clearly marked fictional example showing a question, several different replies and moderator controls. It lives in The Enclave, where real contributions still go through the usual review process.

blocks.title: How do you listen when you already disagree?
blocks.text: Explore a fictional conversation with three sample replies. The example is closed to new replies so it stays distinct from real community discussion.

title: Ibidapo Lawal and the Courage to Learn Again
deck: He had the ambition. Experience supplied the hard lessons. Business school became a turning point. The Neveah founder’s story asks what it takes to build differently the next time.
alt: Ibidapo Lawal in a dark suit and tie, in the portrait supplied for this sample

blocks.text: There is a version of the entrepreneurial story that begins at the breakthrough. The company has a name, the founder has a biography, and the difficult years have been compressed into a sentence about perseverance. Ibidapo Lawal’s story becomes more interesting when you resist that compression.

Before Neveah, there were earlier businesses. Before the polished account of growth, there were setbacks. And somewhere along the way came a decision to return to the classroom—a reminder that ambition can take a man a long way without answering every question he needs to ask.
The ambition came first

Opeyemi Awoyemi, who identifies Lawal as his cousin in a public reflection on his journey, describes a man whose appetite for building was apparent early. Wealth arrived young, he writes, but it did not arrive with a guarantee of permanence. His account describes Lawal as having been bankrupt at least twice.

That detail changes the rhythm of the success story. It introduces a more demanding subject than confidence: the ability to begin again after the evidence has become uncomfortable. To build is to make decisions before the outcome is clear. To rebuild is to do it with a memory of what the last attempt cost.

Awoyemi places a significant turn in that journey at business school in the United States. In his telling, formal education joined an existing mixture of drive, practical intelligence and experience. Watching that combination develop helped shape his own determination to pursue further education.
A different kind of investment

Lawal’s educational path took him from Ibadan to Lead City University, where he studied Economics, and then to Drexel University for an MBA. Both Neveah’s management biography and The Guardian’s October 2024 profile record that progression.

For an entrepreneur, going back to school is an investment with an unusual admission built into it: there are things I do not yet know. Experience brings knowledge, but it can also harden a habit into a rule. A classroom creates an opportunity to place those rules beside other ways of thinking.
The courage to begin again matters. So does the humility to begin differently.

The value of that opportunity is not that a degree removes risk. It is that learning can improve the questions brought to a decision. What is the business actually earning? Which risks are being rewarded, and which are simply being repeated? What survives when the founder is no longer in every room? These are questions for anyone trying to turn personal drive into an enduring institution.
Building beyond the founder

The Guardian traces Lawal’s business activity through IAL Resources and Activo Global Investments, established in 2007, before Neveah’s arrival in 2014. Its profile describes a company exporting solid minerals and agricultural products. Neveah’s own account now places industrial recycling alongside its commodities business.

Those businesses make the story tangible. This is an ambition expressed through products, buyers, exports and industrial activity. The work is less romantic than the language often used to describe entrepreneurship. It involves turning a promise into something another person can depend on, then doing it again.

That is where a founder’s development becomes more than a private achievement. A company is a set of commitments to people who did not share the founder’s original leap of faith: employees, customers, partners and families. Growth increases the number of people affected by the quality of the decisions at the top.
What a setback is for

It is easy to admire resilience after the turnaround. It is harder to recognise the quieter work that makes a turnaround useful: accepting criticism, revising an assumption, asking someone better informed, abandoning a method that once felt inseparable from your identity.

Lawal’s journey offers a way into that conversation. The appeal is not a promise that every failure contains a future fortune. Some mistakes are costly, and some opportunities do not return. The more useful possibility is that a man can take responsibility for what experience has taught him and allow it to change the next attempt.
The next version of ambition

For men taught to equate competence with always knowing the answer, becoming a student again can feel like a loss of standing. Yet a willingness to learn may be one of the strongest expressions of seriousness about the work. The objective is bigger than appearing naturally gifted at it.

The lasting question in Lawal’s story is therefore not simply how much he wanted to succeed. It is what he was willing to change in pursuit of building something that could last. Ambition supplied the movement. Learning gave the journey another direction.

title: Jensen Huang, Our Man of the Year: Greatness Comes With Consequences
deck: He helped change the world. He also let people down. His resignation gives us a harder conversation about achievement, accountability and the limits of a founder’s claim on his company.
alt: Jensen Huang in an official NVIDIA press portrait

blocks.text: A man can build something extraordinary and still fail the people closest to him. Holding those two facts together is uncomfortable. It is also where an honest conversation about leadership has to begin.

Jensen Huang is our Man of the Year because his story now forces that conversation. The builder who became one of the defining figures of the artificial-intelligence era has stepped away from the company he co-founded. His achievements remain. So do the consequences of his choices. Neither cancels the other.
The achievement is real

NVIDIA’s biography dates Huang’s founding of the company to 1993. Across the decades that followed, graphics processors became central to a much wider computing transformation. His career helped put accelerated computing at the heart of an industry that now reaches far beyond gaming.

That is an extraordinary professional legacy. It is also an insufficient answer to a question about conduct. A company’s importance does not make its founder exempt from obligations to family, colleagues or the institution he helped create.
So is the failure

In a November 8 message published by NVIDIA, Huang acknowledged being unfaithful to his wife, apologised to his family and colleagues, and accepted responsibility for the harm he had caused. He also said he supported the board’s independent investigation into national-security concerns raised in reporting.
There is no excuse for what I did.
blocks.attribution: Jensen Huang · message to NVIDIA employees, November 8, 2026

blocks.text: The admission matters. An apology that names the act and the people hurt gives accountability somewhere to begin. It does not finish the work. Trust belongs to the people whose trust was damaged; it cannot be restored by the applause of strangers.
The company has to be bigger than one man

On November 12, NVIDIA announced Huang’s resignation as president, chief executive and director. Colette Kress was appointed interim chief executive, with Harvey C. Jones becoming chair of the board. The company began a search for a permanent successor.

For us, the lesson is the importance of allowing an institution to continue beyond the person most closely associated with it. Founding a company creates a profound relationship. It does not create an unlimited entitlement to lead it. Employees, customers and shareholders have lives and obligations beyond the founder’s story.

The public announcement establishes the transition. It cannot tell us every conversation behind closed doors. We should therefore be careful about turning a resignation into proof of private serenity or claiming that there was no conflict with the board. What we can assess is the public acknowledgement of wrongdoing and the fact that the leadership changed.
What we mean by man of the year

This is an editorial choice, not a declaration of moral perfection. We are interested in a man whose scale of achievement and scale of consequence make the questions impossible to avoid. Did he fail? By his own account, yes. Does acknowledging that failure matter? Yes. Does stepping down erase it? No.

The standard should travel. We would ask the same of Elon Musk, a founder running a small business or a man leading his household: can you hear that you have caused harm without making your status the centre of the conversation? Can you accept a consequence you would rather avoid? The test becomes more demanding as power grows.

There is room to recognise the builder without asking the people hurt by his behaviour to become supporting characters in a redemption story. Their forgiveness is not ours to award. Nor should allegations still under investigation be treated as established findings.
An ending we cannot write yet

Huang may return to a prominent leadership role, or he may not. We do not know. A comeback would not by itself establish repair, just as an absence from the spotlight would not tell us everything about the work being done in private.

What makes this moment worth examining is the boundary it puts around greatness. Talent does not settle every argument. Building an institution does not place a man above it. The ability to change the world must live alongside the willingness to answer for what you do inside it.

title: The Menclave 100: Books Every Man Should Read
deck: A lifetime of reading. One essential list. From Achebe and Austen to Baldwin, Bonhoeffer and the books that change how we live.
alt: Library bookshelves photographed by Priscilla Du Preez

blocks.text: A good book gives you more than something to talk about. It can sharpen your judgement, enlarge your sympathies or put a question into words that you have carried for years. These are 100 books we would make room for in a serious reading life.

The Menclave 100 is our editorial selection, arranged across ten shelves: faith, fiction, work, love, history and the wider world. The numbers help you find your place; the shelves offer different ways in. Start with the question that is most alive for you.

blocks.title: The inner life
blocks.intro: Books that ask who you are when nobody is applauding.

items.title: The Bible
items.author: Various authors
items.note: A library of lament, poetry, law, wisdom and redemption. Read whole books in context, and make room for the passages that resist an easy answer.

items.title: Meditations
items.author: Marcus Aurelius
items.note: An emperor tries to govern his own reactions. Keep it close when your attention is being pulled towards everything except your responsibilities.

items.title: Confessions
items.author: Augustine of Hippo
items.note: Restlessness becomes a sustained examination of memory, desire and belief. Its lasting challenge is the willingness to tell the truth about yourself.

items.title: Man’s Search for Meaning
items.author: Viktor E. Frankl
items.note: Frankl’s account of imprisonment and his reflections on meaning ask what remains possible when control over circumstances has been brutally reduced.

items.title: The Brothers Karamazov
items.author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
items.note: Fathers, sons, faith and moral responsibility collide in a novel large enough to make certainty feel inadequate. Give the arguments time to work on you.

items.title: Things Fall Apart
items.author: Chinua Achebe
items.note: Okonkwo’s fear of weakness becomes inseparable from his tragedy. A foundational novel for thinking about masculinity, belonging and the violence of colonial disruption.

items.title: Invisible Man
items.author: Ralph Ellison
items.note: A young man discovers how readily institutions turn a person into a symbol. Read it for the voice, the anger and the struggle to define yourself.

items.title: The Death of Ivan Ilyich
items.author: Leo Tolstoy
items.note: A respectable life faces an uncomfortable reckoning. This short work asks whether being admired and living well have quietly become different projects.

items.title: The Fire Next Time
items.author: James Baldwin
items.note: Personal address becomes a searching examination of race, religion and America. Baldwin demands an honesty that refuses both innocence and easy hatred.

items.title: Mere Christianity
items.author: C. S. Lewis
items.note: A clear, argumentative introduction to Christian belief. Read it as a conversation partner: follow the reasoning, examine its assumptions and bring your own questions.

blocks.title: Faith, doubt & grace
blocks.intro: A shelf for conviction that can survive a difficult question.

items.title: Gilead
items.author: Marilynne Robinson
items.note: An ageing minister writes to his young son. Its quiet attention to blessing, jealousy and forgiveness makes an ordinary life feel worthy of deep examination.

items.title: The Pilgrim’s Progress
items.author: John Bunyan
items.note: Spiritual struggle takes the shape of a journey. Beneath the allegory is a recognisable account of discouragement, distraction and the need for companions.

items.title: Silence
items.author: Shūsaku Endō
items.note: Faith meets persecution and the terrible ambiguity of another person’s suffering. A demanding novel that offers no convenient distance from its central dilemma.

items.title: The Cost of Discipleship
items.author: Dietrich Bonhoeffer
items.note: An insistence that belief has consequences for how a person lives. Read slowly, with attention to the historical pressures surrounding its author.

items.title: The Return of the Prodigal Son
items.author: Henri J. M. Nouwen
items.note: A painting becomes a way to examine resentment, belonging and mercy. Especially valuable for anyone who finds receiving love harder than earning approval.

items.title: Orthodoxy
items.author: G. K. Chesterton
items.note: A lively defence of Christian belief through paradox and surprise. Its energy rewards readers willing to wrestle with an argument rather than simply inherit it.

items.title: The Screwtape Letters
items.author: C. S. Lewis
items.note: Temptation appears through distraction, vanity and small evasions. The fictional correspondence is sharpest when its spiritual diagnosis becomes embarrassingly familiar.

items.title: The Cross and the Lynching Tree
items.author: James H. Cone
items.note: Christian theology confronts the history of racial terror in America. A necessary challenge to faith that speaks of suffering while avoiding its victims.

items.title: The Prophetic Imagination
items.author: Walter Brueggemann
items.note: Scripture becomes a resource for challenging numbness and imagining a different social order. It asks what hope demands from public life.

items.title: The Dignity of Difference
items.author: Jonathan Sacks
items.note: An argument for living with religious difference without abandoning conviction. Read it for the difficult work of finding moral responsibility across boundaries.

blocks.title: Work, money & ambition
blocks.intro: What success asks of you, and what it can cost.

items.title: Macbeth
items.author: William Shakespeare
items.note: Ambition crosses a moral threshold and discovers that power cannot quiet fear. A brief, devastating study of the next compromise.

items.title: The Great Gatsby
items.author: F. Scott Fitzgerald
items.note: Reinvention, longing and wealth gather around a dream that cannot survive scrutiny. The beautiful surfaces make the emptiness underneath more unsettling.

items.title: Death of a Salesman
items.author: Arthur Miller
items.note: A man’s idea of success leaves little room for his actual life. Read it with attention to what families inherit from a father’s disappointments.

items.title: The Remains of the Day
items.author: Kazuo Ishiguro
items.note: Professional duty becomes a shelter from emotional and moral responsibility. A restrained novel about the terrible cost of recognising things late.

items.title: The Intelligent Investor
items.author: Benjamin Graham
items.note: A classic argument for discipline and caution in investing. Read for its approach to risk and judgement, while recognising that market practices and examples age.

items.title: The Psychology of Money
items.author: Morgan Housel
items.note: Short reflections on how behaviour shapes financial decisions. A useful prompt to define enough before comparison defines it for you.

items.title: The Wealth of Nations
items.author: Adam Smith
items.note: A foundational work on commerce, labour and economic organisation. Read it in historical context and attend to its arguments rather than its reputation.

items.title: Good to Great
items.author: Jim Collins
items.note: An influential account of organisational performance. Treat the cases as material for critical discussion, with hindsight and selection effects firmly in view.

items.title: Shoe Dog
items.author: Phil Knight
items.note: A founder’s memoir of building Nike through uncertainty. Best read alongside questions about whose labour and risk make a company’s origin story possible.

items.title: The Soul of a New Machine
items.author: Tracy Kidder
items.note: Engineering becomes an intimate story of work, pressure and collective effort. It makes the people inside a technical achievement visible.

blocks.title: Love, family & friendship
blocks.intro: The books that make other people harder to simplify.

items.title: Anna Karenina
items.author: Leo Tolstoy
items.note: Desire, marriage and social judgement unfold across an enormous moral landscape. Its power comes from refusing to reduce people to their worst decision.

items.title: Middlemarch
items.author: George Eliot
items.note: Private hopes meet the limits of knowledge, marriage and community. Few novels are more attentive to the distance between good intentions and useful care.

items.title: Pride and Prejudice
items.author: Jane Austen
items.note: First impressions become an education in judgement. Read the wit closely: pride, money and self-knowledge are doing serious work underneath it.

items.title: Beloved
items.author: Toni Morrison
items.note: The afterlife of slavery enters a family’s struggle to live. A formally daring novel about memory, love and injuries that exceed easy explanation.

items.title: Little Women
items.author: Louisa May Alcott
items.note: Sisters negotiate work, independence and family loyalty. A useful widening of perspective for men whose reading rarely follows women’s ambitions from the inside.

items.title: All About Love
items.author: bell hooks
items.note: An argument that love is a practice with ethical demands. Read it as an invitation to examine what your habits are actually offering others.

items.title: The Art of Loving
items.author: Erich Fromm
items.note: Love becomes a discipline of attention, knowledge and responsibility. Its central provocation is that wanting to be loved is only a beginning.

items.title: The Four Loves
items.author: C. S. Lewis
items.note: Affection, friendship, romance and charity receive distinct attention. A thoughtful companion for examining what each relationship can reasonably ask of another person.

items.title: The Road
items.author: Cormac McCarthy
items.note: A father and son travel through a devastated world. Its spare language makes care feel urgent, fragile and stubbornly necessary.

items.title: Between the World and Me
items.author: Ta-Nehisi Coates
items.note: A father addresses his son through history and bodily vulnerability. The letter form gives its larger questions an immediate, personal weight.

blocks.title: Home, identity & the wider world
blocks.intro: A reading life should have more than one centre.

items.title: Half of a Yellow Sun
items.author: Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie
items.note: Intimate relationships unfold through the Biafran War. The novel makes political catastrophe legible through the lives and loyalties it tears apart.

items.title: So Long a Letter
items.author: Mariama Bâ
items.note: A widow’s letter examines marriage, friendship and women’s independence. Its intimacy makes structural inequality impossible to dismiss as an abstract concern.

items.title: Season of Migration to the North
items.author: Tayeb Salih
items.note: A return home opens a disturbing reckoning with colonial encounter, desire and power. A short novel that leaves a long argument behind.

items.title: Petals of Blood
items.author: Ngũgĩ wa Thiong’o
items.note: Lives intersect in a searching critique of postcolonial power and economic betrayal. Read it for the connection between private wounds and public arrangements.

items.title: Cry, the Beloved Country
items.author: Alan Paton
items.note: A father’s search opens onto a divided South Africa. Its attention to grief and reconciliation invites both empathy and historical scrutiny.

items.title: The Famished Road
items.author: Ben Okri
items.note: A spirit-child narrates a world where the visible and unseen continually meet. The novel expands what a story about everyday survival can hold.

items.title: Nervous Conditions
items.author: Tsitsi Dangarembga
items.note: Education, gender and colonial power shape a young woman’s effort to define her life. An incisive book about the costs attached to opportunity.

items.title: One Hundred Years of Solitude
items.author: Gabriel García Márquez
items.note: A family’s history turns through wonder, violence and repetition. Read for the extraordinary way the fantastic can illuminate a recognisable social world.

items.title: The God of Small Things
items.author: Arundhati Roy
items.note: Family memory is shaped by caste, politics and forbidden love. Its language attends to the small details through which larger systems enter a life.

items.title: The Kite Runner
items.author: Khaled Hosseini
items.note: Friendship and betrayal become a reckoning with guilt across distance and time. Its emotional force rests on the question of what repair can require.

blocks.title: Courage, conflict & conscience
blocks.intro: Accounts of what people endure, and what they choose.

items.title: The Iliad
items.author: Homer
items.note: War is seen through rage, grief and the limits of glory. Read beyond the battles to the moments when an enemy becomes recognisably human.

items.title: The Odyssey
items.author: Homer
items.note: Adventure is also a story of homecoming, loyalty and disguise. Returning home proves more complicated than surviving the journey.

items.title: War and Peace
items.author: Leo Tolstoy
items.note: Private lives move inside vast historical forces. The novel unsettles tidy ideas about control, greatness and the people who supposedly make history.

items.title: All Quiet on the Western Front
items.author: Erich Maria Remarque
items.note: A young soldier’s experience strips war of its recruiting language. Read it before making sacrifice sound simple from a safe distance.

items.title: Catch-22
items.author: Joseph Heller
items.note: Military bureaucracy becomes a darkly comic system that consumes reason. Its absurdity is a way of seeing how institutions protect themselves.

items.title: Slaughterhouse-Five
items.author: Kurt Vonnegut
items.note: A fractured narrative returns to war and the difficulty of representing it. The broken chronology is part of the book’s moral force.

items.title: If This Is a Man
items.author: Primo Levi
items.note: Levi’s account of Auschwitz examines survival and the destruction of human dignity. Precision and restraint make the testimony profoundly demanding.

items.title: Night
items.author: Elie Wiesel
items.note: A brief account of the Holocaust confronts suffering, family and faith. Give its testimony attention without trying to turn it into a reassuring lesson.

items.title: Long Walk to Freedom
items.author: Nelson Mandela
items.note: A political life is narrated through struggle, imprisonment and collective purpose. Read with attention to the long work behind public symbols.

items.title: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass
items.author: Frederick Douglass
items.note: Literacy, resistance and self-emancipation drive a foundational autobiography. Its clarity exposes the violence required to sustain a system of enslavement.

blocks.title: Power, freedom & justice
blocks.intro: A shelf for becoming a more demanding citizen.

items.title: The Republic
items.author: Plato
items.note: Justice becomes a sustained argument about the person and the state. Its proposals invite challenge as much as admiration.

items.title: Nicomachean Ethics
items.author: Aristotle
items.note: Character is examined through habit, judgement and the shape of a good life. A durable starting point for thinking beyond isolated good intentions.

items.title: On Liberty
items.author: John Stuart Mill
items.note: An influential defence of individual freedom and open discussion. Its boundaries remain useful material for arguments about responsibility and social power.

items.title: Nineteen Eighty-Four
items.author: George Orwell
items.note: Surveillance and political language become tools for remaking reality. Read for the intimate effects of power as well as its famous vocabulary.

items.title: Brave New World
items.author: Aldous Huxley
items.note: Comfort and conditioning support an unsettling social order. The book asks what freedom means when desire itself has been organised for you.

items.title: Animal Farm
items.author: George Orwell
items.note: A revolution’s promises are steadily rewritten by those who inherit power. Its simplicity makes the mechanisms of betrayal unusually clear.

items.title: The Trial
items.author: Franz Kafka
items.note: An accusation arrives without a comprehensible system of justice. The unease comes from watching a person search for rules that keep receding.

items.title: The Plague
items.author: Albert Camus
items.note: An epidemic turns ordinary obligations into moral choices. Its most enduring interest is the patient, unglamorous work of solidarity.

items.title: The Origins of Totalitarianism
items.author: Hannah Arendt
items.note: A major investigation of the conditions and forms of totalitarian power. Read critically and in conversation with later historical scholarship.

items.title: The New Jim Crow
items.author: Michelle Alexander
items.note: A forceful argument about racial inequality and mass incarceration in the United States. It invites close attention to systems that outlast their official language.

blocks.title: Adventure & the imagination
blocks.intro: Books that make the world larger.

items.title: Don Quixote
items.author: Miguel de Cervantes
items.note: A reader ventures out with an imagination that refuses the world’s corrections. Comic adventure becomes a meditation on stories and friendship.

items.title: Moby-Dick
items.author: Herman Melville
items.note: A voyage gathers obsession, labour, knowledge and a dangerous concentration of authority. Let its strange digressions become part of the journey.

items.title: The Lord of the Rings
items.author: J. R. R. Tolkien
items.note: A vast imagined world turns on friendship, endurance and the corrupting pull of power. Small acts matter within its enormous stakes.

items.title: The Hobbit
items.author: J. R. R. Tolkien
items.note: Comfort gives way to adventure, and an unlikely traveller discovers courage. A generous reminder that bravery need not arrive looking impressive.

items.title: Dune
items.author: Frank Herbert
items.note: Ecology, religion and political ambition meet in an immense speculative world. Read attentively to its questions about leaders and the people who follow them.

items.title: The Left Hand of Darkness
items.author: Ursula K. Le Guin
items.note: An unfamiliar society becomes a way to examine gender, loyalty and understanding. The journey rewards readers willing to have their assumptions unsettled.

items.title: Frankenstein
items.author: Mary Shelley
items.note: Creation brings obligations that ambition would rather avoid. A powerful novel about responsibility, rejection and the consequences of abandoning what you make.

items.title: The Count of Monte Cristo
items.author: Alexandre Dumas
items.note: Revenge supplies the engine for a magnificent adventure. Beneath the momentum is a question about what a long grievance does to a life.

items.title: Treasure Island
items.author: Robert Louis Stevenson
items.note: A map launches an adventure full of danger and uncertain loyalties. Read it for the storytelling pleasure of a world suddenly opening up.

items.title: The Old Man and the Sea
items.author: Ernest Hemingway
items.note: An ageing fisherman’s struggle becomes a spare examination of endurance and pride. Its scale is small enough for every action to carry weight.

blocks.title: Craft, attention & the everyday
blocks.intro: Learning to see what a hurried life misses.

items.title: Walden
items.author: Henry David Thoreau
items.note: An experiment in living becomes a challenge to habitual definitions of need. Read it with curiosity about both its insights and its practical circumstances.

items.title: A Sand County Almanac
items.author: Aldo Leopold
items.note: Close observation develops into an ethic of ecological responsibility. A book for learning to see land as a living relationship.

items.title: Pilgrim at Tinker Creek
items.author: Annie Dillard
items.note: The natural world receives fierce, unsettling attention. Dillard makes looking closely feel like an intellectual and spiritual discipline.

items.title: The Creative Act
items.author: Rick Rubin
items.note: Short meditations consider attention, making and creative practice. Dip into it when you need to return to the work without demanding a guaranteed outcome.

items.title: On Writing
items.author: Stephen King
items.note: Memoir meets practical advice about the craft of writing. Most useful when its lessons send you back to a page of your own.

items.title: Bird by Bird
items.author: Anne Lamott
items.note: A humane account of writing through doubt and imperfect beginnings. Read it when the size of a project has become an excuse not to start.

items.title: On Writing Well
items.author: William Zinsser
items.note: Clarity is treated as a discipline of thought and revision. Its usefulness extends to anyone whose work depends on being understood.

items.title: Working
items.author: Studs Terkel
items.note: Oral histories reveal how people experience their jobs. The range of voices makes work harder to reduce to a title or salary.

items.title: A Sense of Where You Are
items.author: John McPhee
items.note: A close portrait of basketball player Bill Bradley becomes a study of preparation and attention. Excellence appears through specific habits rather than slogans.

items.title: Amusing Ourselves to Death
items.author: Neil Postman
items.note: A critique of television asks how a medium changes public thought. Read it alongside questions about the attention habits of your own era.

blocks.title: Memory, mortality & a life well lived
blocks.intro: The final shelf returns us to the people we become.

items.title: East of Eden
items.author: John Steinbeck
items.note: Family history becomes an expansive exploration of inheritance and choice. Its moral questions are strongest when they remain attached to imperfect people.

items.title: The Grapes of Wrath
items.author: John Steinbeck
items.note: A displaced family travels through economic hardship and exclusion. The novel insists on the human consequences of arrangements often described impersonally.

items.title: Stoner
items.author: John Williams
items.note: An apparently unremarkable academic life receives extraordinary attention. A quiet novel about vocation, limitation and what counts as a life worth telling.

items.title: A Single Man
items.author: Christopher Isherwood
items.note: One day in a grieving man’s life becomes a precise account of loneliness and connection. Its compressed form makes ordinary encounters carry unusual force.

items.title: A Small Place
items.author: Jamaica Kincaid
items.note: A sharp address to the visitor unsettles comfortable ways of seeing Antigua. A brief book that asks readers to examine the position from which they look.

items.title: The Autobiography of Malcolm X
items.author: Malcolm X with Alex Haley
items.note: A life is narrated through repeated transformations of conviction and identity. Read it for the willingness to revise an understanding of the world.

items.title: When Breath Becomes Air
items.author: Paul Kalanithi
items.note: A neurosurgeon confronts terminal illness and the limits of professional mastery. The memoir asks what makes life meaningful when its horizon changes.

items.title: Being Mortal
items.author: Atul Gawande
items.note: Ageing and serious illness become questions about priorities, care and autonomy. Read for the conversations it may help you begin with people you love.

items.title: The Year of Magical Thinking
items.author: Joan Didion
items.note: Grief is examined through the mind’s attempts to bargain with loss. Its precision offers company without pretending to tidy the experience away.

items.title: The Little Prince
items.author: Antoine de Saint-Exupéry
items.note: A small fable opens large questions about friendship, care and attention. Return to it when adulthood has made the measurable seem like the only thing that matters.

blocks.text: Choose your next book, not your next hundred

Pick one that challenges your habits and one you will enjoy returning to. Read at a pace that allows the book to leave a mark. Keep a sentence, argue with an idea, lend a copy to a friend. A reading life is made by the attention you give it.

blocks.title: Which book would you add?
blocks.text: Tell us the book that changed how you see the world—and what stayed with you. This conversation is open for replies.
